REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 1
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
Last evening while I was dealing with the winter works program, I was interrupted, as usual, by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay). At one point, I did not quite catch what he had said, but this morning, on going over Hansard, I find on page 1690 (page 4 of the appendix) that he said this:

subtopic: REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 1
speechtext:
Yes. Is it for that reason that the hon. member is trying to protect certain very dubious individuals in my constituency? Criminals?
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I have ever protected any criminals, and have no intention of doing so either now or in the future. That remark on the part of the hon. member is a reflection on my good name as member of the House of Commons and I would ask that you kindly request the member for Roberval to withdraw those words.
(Text):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 1
speechtext:
The hon. member raises today a question of privilege arising out of something that was said last night. Normally that would not be in order. Questions of privilege which arise in this way in the course of debate must be taken up at once. After they have become a matter of record it is rather late. The hon. member indicates that he did not hear what was said at the time. I am not sure whether there is any real reflection on the hon. member involved in what was said, but as he has complained I will give the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay) an opportunity to comment on it.
(Translation):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening, when the member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) was making a speech on the employment situation in Canada, he took the liberty of referring to my riding, to which I obviously cannot object. That is exactly what I said. I said it because I had reasons for doing so, and I undertake to state in the house, when we take up the items of the Department of Justice, what I had in mind.

speechtext: I heard the hon. member in the first instance. I doubt that there is sufficient cause for complaint in what he said. I will not direct the hon. member to do something which he does not wish to do voluntarily.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 1
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise on this question of privilege and point out to you that yesterday I had to withdraw a statement made under exactly the same circumstances when, in asking a question of the Chairman, I insinuated that he was using two different weights and measures as between the opposition and the government. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: WORLD REFUGEE YEAR
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ADMIS- SION OF ADDITIONAL REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an announcement about the participation of the government in world refugee year through the admission of tuberculous refugees and their families to Canada.
I am pleased to report that the 100 families already admitted have shown a remarkable ability to integrate rapidly into Canadian
1640	HOUSE OF
Admission of Refugees
society. Some of the tuberculous cases have already been discharged from hospital and, with the modern methods of treatment available in Canada, it appears that most of the remaining cases will be discharged within the next two months. Few of the refugees afflicted with this illness will require prolonged treatment. It is also evident that all but a handful of the refugee families will become almost entirely self-supporting within two or three months.
I should like to stress that the choice of the 100 families which have been admitted was left entirely to the high commissioner for refugees. The government was prepared to accept the most serious cases should the high commissioner have thought it helpful to move them from their present locations in Europe.
This project for the admission of tuberculous refugees involved many novel problems for the Canadian authorities. Accordingly it was decided that at the outset the number of families to be admitted should be limited so that an appreciation of the precise problems could be obtained. Since a workable procedure has now been developed for rehabilitating these families, and since the period of treatment and integration has proved shorter than originally estimated, the government has decided to authorize the admission of additional families.
Tuberculous refugees in European camps have various destinations in mind for emigration, and the number wishing to come to Canada is not unlimited. Our representative in Geneva is now consulting with the high commissioner for refugees concerning the availability of additional numbers for inclusion in an extension of the original scheme.
Statements which have been made by representatives of several provinces lead us to believe that a number of provinces are prepared to join with the federal government in an extension of the original program on _ a basis similar to that which was worked out in connection with the first 100 families.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, hon. members will agree that by originating and extending the program for admission of tuberculous refugees, Canada is making a substantial contribution toward the solution of one of the most difficult aspects of the refugee problem, which is the resettlement of the "hard core" cases.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: WORLD REFUGEE YEAR
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ADMIS- SION OF ADDITIONAL REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the house will welcome the decision of the federal government to add to its responsibilities in respect of the admission of handicapped and tubercular refugees. I hope every effort will be made with the provincial


governments in so organizing things that this desirable movement may be carried out as far as possible, and that we will continue to do our share in liquidating this problem which has been with us now for so many years.
I would also express the hope that in considering the admission of additional refugees the government might not restrict the number to refugees in Europe, but that if cases can be found in Asia which are admissible in this category-there will be no discrimination against those cases from there.

subtopic: WORLD REFUGEE YEAR
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ADMIS- SION OF ADDITIONAL REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a number of months we in this group have been indicating that Canada should be more lenient in taking a larger number of refugees into our country. Therefore we are particularly pleased with the attitude taken and the announcement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
He mentioned that some provinces appear to be prepared to go along with the announcement. I express the hope that some consultation has already taken place. This was one objection raised by Saskatchewan to the procedure that has been taken although, as I am sure the minister will agree, Saskatchewan was most pleased to co-operate in this undertaking. As the minister is no doubt aware, the Commonwealth of Australia has been most lenient in its immigration policy, much more so than our country, and we welcome the minister's announcement today.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORTED DECISION TO ESTABLISH MOBILE
speechtext:
Possibly I could answer that question. NATO, in addition to having the capability of waging full scale war, must be prepared to react instantly and in appropriate strength to other aggression against NATO territory.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at ten o'clock last night, when speaking on this item, I suggested to the committee that it might be advisable for a public debate to take place on this matter in Elliot Lake, and I suggested that debate could possibly take place among the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Leader of the Opposition and myself. In thinking about this matter I have come to the conclusion that it would be advisable for the Minister of Labour at least to attend the debate, so he could receive the benefit of the opinions that might be expressed from the floor by the people at that time. If he also wished to debate the matter at that time, all well and good.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that a number of members have made some constructive suggestions. I feel that while the suggestions I have made may not be the complete answer, they should be given some consideration. I have visited Elliot Lake and talked to the people there, and I use Elliot Lake only as an example. I believe this displacement problem is something that is found throughout the whole mining industry. It is not seasonal unemployment; it is unemployment that develops in an area, and it is seldom or ever solved in that area. I suggest something that could be done to solve it in Elliot Lake, because everybody is interested in Elliot Lake. If the suggestions were put into effect in Elliot Lake I am sure they would also apply to Cape Breton Island, to the gold mining industry in the communities of Kirkland Lake and Timmins, and in other places. Probably in the future we shall be faced with the same problem in Sudbury and all the mining communities. Therefore I suggest we should have a discussion of it.
I am worried about some of the things I learned in Elliot Lake when I was there last week end. One of them was the fact

that the people of Elliot Lake have not the answer as to what should be done in this particular instance. Some of them suggest that the solution to the whole problem would be to produce uranium at the same rate as under the present five-year contract. This would mean that the miners would continue to work in exactly the same way. But, Mr. Chairman, all of us know that these things cannot be; that the former government underestimated the market for uranium; that the situation that was expected did not develop in that field, and therefore there does not appear to be any possibility of continuing things as they were or maintaining the status quo.
The ladies who came to Ottawa are to be commended very strongly on the fact that they took the initiative and came here on their own and asked what was to be done or what would be done. They made some suggestions, and I am sure the suggestions are going to be taken into consideration in the light of developments that have taken place in other areas.
I am pleased to see that they are going to the province of Manitoba to ask that province to relinquish any advantage that has been given to it through having this research centre that has been widely spoken of, and return it to the province of Ontario and in particular to Elliot Lake. If this project were brought into Elliot Lake it would not solve the whole problem; it would solve only a small percentage of the problem. Therefore I suggest that consideration be given to a problem which is much wider, and which has a wider application than even Elliot Lake.
With this in mind I strongly urge the Minister of Labour to give consideration to the setting up of a manpower resources board to engage in the retraining and re-establishment of workers on a voluntary basis in areas where their talents and their training would be used to advantage. To this end the government could co-operate with the department and with the unemployment insurance commission, which is now engaged in a small way in retraining and re-establishing workers.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the establishment of a natural industry planning board is the answer to all areas of displacement which have taken place in the last few years. If this board were given wide powers to study and ascertain the resources and materials available in a given area where a town is already established, it would find that certain natural resources would be available in that area that would be advantageous. If we gave them the advantages, as I have suggested, that have been given to the new mining companies, such as a tax-free period when they would 79951-0-104
Supply-Labour
have access to credit that would allow them to develop in that area provided by the federal government, where they would have other concessions that have been given to the mining companies including the speeding up of amortization and depreciation, those companies would find a big advantage in settling in the mining communities that have been developed across the country. I think this could be a much greater contribution to those communities than the subventions and subsidies that have been paid in the past to accomplish the same thing but without achieving nearly the results that were expected from the amount of money spent in this way.
I think the minister has been given some constructive suggestions. With this in mind I repeat that I will be quite happy to go to Elliot Lake, a focal point so far as this problem is concerned, and debate the suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition the other night and replied to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I would be happy to debate with them at Elliot Lake and let the people of Elliot Lake express their opinions. I am quite sure that the three people taking part in the debate would receive a great deal of information and worth-while guidance from the people in that area if they were given the three positions, as I am sure they would be.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, it is almost a month now since the supplementary estimates were introduced, which would authorize this government to spend certain amounts for winter works to help the unemployed.
We might have expected that an item of a few millions, representing a very small fraction of the total budget, would be passed after nothing more than a pro forma discussion and the customary explanations of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). Things turned out otherwise, which is unfortunate for those who are out of work, and, after several days of sterile discussion, during which this house was the scene of a talking marathon, hon. members of the opposition gave forth a torrent of words in which we would look in vain for some constructive suggestion. There are, of course, the 10 points set out by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). We already had "Martin's Bureau of Statistics", and now we shall have "Martin's 10 commandments", which mainly consist in a request that a committee be instituted to consider what might be considered.
Even the young and brilliant member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) made a contribution yesterday, though he had promised never to use unemployment as a political football. One

Supply-Labour
would think that his leaders forced him to break his promise. Aware as I am of his talent and of his usual regard for objectivity, I know that the hon. member for Lapointe is not very proud of the remarks he made yesterday. There was, indeed, a time when he knew how to be realistic and constructive, and refrained from personal attacks like those he directed yesterday against the head of this government.
I do not propose to follow in the steps of the opposition speakers by making useless digressions, so I shall get right into the subject matter which is of interest to all of us, that is, unemployment.
There has been a lot of talk stressing the tragedy of Elliot Lake, and I personally have great sympathy for the residents of that community which is so deeply affected by the cutback in uranium production. However, I remember that, in 1929, under a Liberal administration, the pulp mills of Chicoutimi closed down, and our city found itself precisely in the same position as Elliot Lake today.
I wonder if among Liberal party veterans there is a single one who, at that time, expressed a single word of sympathy for our community, which was also in danger of becoming a ghost town. Without the courage, the determination and the enterprise of our people, it actually would have become one.
I remember, for having lived through it, the period from 1929 to 1939, when most of the people back home were out of work. I know what tragedies unemployment can lead to. To me, unemployment is not merely of academic interest, nor is it a matter of statistics; because the unemployed worker and all his family suffer even when statistics indicate favourable overall conditions.
The right to work in a country full of resources, that can afford to absorb millions of immigrants and to finance underdeveloped countries, is an essential right which should be embodied if not in the constitution, at least in the bill of rights, because liberty, freedom of speech, the right to practise one's own religion and to speak one's own language remain empty words if workers cannot make a living. Otherwise they only remain free to starve democratically and legally.
Does this mean that this government has done nothing to check unemployment? On the contrary, without the bold steps taken

by our government, the situation would be much worse. For instance, the unprecedented amounts of money made available to the building industry may be doubly considered as funds designed to check unemployment. In fact, those funds have made it possible to hire large numbers of workers in the building trades, and have at the same time helped industry generally, by putting building materials to use. In the constituency of Chicoutimi alone, for instance, it is not exaggerated to state that more houses were built in two years and a half of Conservative administration than during the whole previous Liberal administration. That is, it seems to me, a way of checking unemployment, although opposition members may claim that nothing has been done.
As I should like to be brief, Mr. Chairman, I shall come at once to the practical conclusions, suggestions requested last evening by the Minister of Labour. It seems to me that the basic weakness of our economy is that we can achieve full employment only in war time and that, so long as we are at peace, we cannot provide work for all of our workers.
Of course, account must be taken of the fact that Canada is a country which has to export, and that export markets are necessarily unsteady. However, Mr. Chairman, with a little imagination, we could find a formula that could allow us to provide jobs for all our workers, without upsetting the federal budget, or ruining our provinces and municipalities. To achieve that objective, I would suggest the adoption of a job insurance scheme that would replace our present unemployment insurance program. As things now stand, as soon as a worker is out of work, provided he qualifies, he gets unemployment benefits for a number of weeks.
Millions are thus spent every year to keep people idle and get them into the habit of loafing. With a contribution that might perhaps be slightly higher than the one now paid by employers and workers, there would be enough money in the fund to undertake useful works that would beautify and enrich our country, while providing employment for all who are temporarily out of jobs in industry or business.
I know that employers and workers would all be quite happy to pay a higher contribution, providing it would rid them for-

ever of the spectre of unemployment- The mere fact of undertaking works, purchasing materials and generally distributing purchasing power would revitalize industry generally, and probably in a short time, the employment insurance agency would have no workers available to pursue its works, except in isolated cases, such as Elliot Lake.
Another consideration of a psychological nature, is that the worker would be much happier earning his living than wilting away, with or without unemployment insurance benefits.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the practical suggestion I wanted to make to the Minister of Labour. And I hope that, until my suggestion is considered further, the requested funds will be voted without delay to relieve the present situation.

May I ask the hon. member a question before he resumes his seat? I believe he said that, in his opinion, the right to work is a fundamental one. Is he in favour of including this right to work in the bill of rights that the Prime Minister plans to introduce?

Mr. Chairman, I do not feel authorized to announce government policy, but if I may express a personal opinion, I would say: Yes, I do favour including it.

Is the minister, in effect, now saying that what he, the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs proposed when they were on this side of the house was proposed under false pretences to fool the people of this country or did they mean what they said? If they meant what they said, then they should listen to the constructive suggestions which were made by my hon. friend the member for Essex East.
I now want to put succinctly on the Hansard record the proposals which were made by those of us who sit on this side of the house. Of course, it will not be possible for me to list them all but I have selected 25 and I would ask the minister to take note and listen to them.
1.	Responsibility for unemployment, in the face of the present emergency, should be taken from the Department of Labour and transferred to the government as a whole.
2.	Canada should have a national advisory board on economic development, automation and employment to help deal with long term problems of production and employment.
3.	Appointment of a special parliamentary committee to assess the effects of unemployment and to explore ways and means of dealing with the problem, as advocated by the Progressive Conservatives while they sat in opposition.

4.	A federal-provincial conference on unemployment, as advocated by the Progressive Conservatives when they were in opposition.
5.	The government should call a conference of industry and labour to discuss and examine the unemployment problem, as suggested by the Canadian Labour Congress and by Les Syndicats Catholiques.
6.	Immediate consideration be given to the utilization of the services of an outstanding businessman, who has a knowledge of the problem and the capacity to provide leadership in supplying jobs.
7.	Modification of the winter works program to make it more acceptable to municipalities, as recommended by the conference of mayors and municipalities.
8.	The government, as a whole, not just the Minister of Labour, should concentrate its attention on surplus areas of unemployment to assess the economic factors and to establish methods of providing work in those areas.
9.	Intensification of the vocational training program to provide necessary skills for the unemployed in the surplus areas and generally throughout the country.
10.	The government should establish an Atlantic provinces capital assistance fund in order to finance large projects essential to sound economic development.
11.	Modification of the 50-50 sharing formula to give greater assistance to provinces and municipalities with heavy unemployment and a small capacity to pay.
12.	The planning of the winter works program earlier so that the municipalities might get projects ready in time, as we recommended in August, 1958, and again in May and June, 1959.
13.	Special assistance to the Atlantic provinces for the building of highways and not just roads to resources.
14.	The whole public works and construction program should be planned and timed to provide maximum employment in the winter months.
15.	Vocational training of the unemployed should be paid for by the federal government on a basis similar to the veterans training and education at the end of the war.
16.	The Prime Minister should carry out his pledge to the textile workers of Canada.
17.	The government should not curtail housing in the face of unemployment.

18.	The government should approach the province of Quebec to the end of getting them to co-operate in the roads to resources program and other similar programs.
19.	The government should pay 90 per cent of the cost of the trans-Canada highway in the Atlantic provinces to speed up construction and provide employment.
20.	The government should accept at once the recommendations of the fisheries council regarding fishing vessels including subventions for vessels built in Canada.
21.	The government should provide subventions on coal for industrial purposes in the Atlantic provinces equal to the subvention paid on coal shipped to Montreal.
22.	The government should carry out the national resources development program promised in the Atlantic resolutions.
23.	The government should carry out decentralization of industry as promised in the Atlantic resolutions.
24.	The government should carry out its pledge to reduce transportation costs in the Atlantic provinces to give them access to the markets of central Canada.
25.	The government should establish a municipal loan fund.
Then I would bring to the attention of the minister-and I hope he will deal with it when he rises-an editorial which appeared in last night's Journal dealing with this debate and dealing with the whole subject of winter unemployment, and the suggestion made in the last paragraph but one of the editorial which reads as follows:
But what we feel might help would be a special study of winter unemployment, of steps to cope with it, or to cope with it as far as possible.

speechtext: If that table is carefully examined it will be seen that from the period 1946 to 1956-10 years-the average annual percentage of the labour force without jobs in Canada was 2.8 per cent.

I say that during that time that average was 2.8 per cent; and I bring to the attention of the committee the fact that the experts in the field say that 3 per cent of the labour force without jobs is the eauivalent of full employment.
That was the position as it was then. I draw this table to the attention of the hon. member for St. Mary who had some comment to make on it. I hope he will take the trouble to look at it and see for himself that it is taken from the statistics of the government.
I say that if the Minister of Labour and the government find themselves in the position in which they are now it is owing in large measure to their own policies in the fiscal and the monetary fields. As we know, there was a recession in 1957 and the former administration dealt with a similar recession in a clear and straightforward manner. That is not the first time there has been a recession in this country. There was also one in 1953; and
[The Chairman.]
during the course of that recession we refused to increase our long term financial commitments. We chose instead to reduce taxes.
The present administration, in order to meet the recession of 1957 chose to increase its long term expenditures instead of reducing taxes. It chose to deal with the recession just as if it were a depression. This method has had disastrous consequences such as those from which we are still suffering.
Let us see what happened. First, long term public expenditures, as we know, particularly in the field of public works, do not have the immediate effect of coming to the assistance of those who are in dire need- as are the unemployed-in the same manner as does a reduction in taxation.
Next, the increase in long term expenditures cannot easily be stopped once they are started, with the result that instead of bringing about a temporary deficit we have a long line of deficits such as those we had since this government has been in office. Thus, the budgetary and non-budgetary deficit in 1957-58 amounted to $160 million; in 1958-59, $1,250 million; in 1959-60, $850 million and in 1960-61 it will probably be in the nature of $400 million. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that this series of deficits is at the origin of all our financial problems. In 1958, in the face of this deficitary position, the government decided to sell a new series of government bonds and by doing that created a serious condition on the market.
In order to help the government finance its position, the Bank of Canada had to increase the monetary supply. It increased the supply by $1,700 million, an increase of 16 per cent. This caused an inflationary situation and the Bank of Canada had to stop its monetary expansion. Then the government found itself in competition with private enterprise, with the corporations, with municipalities and the like, in its desire to get funds in the open market in order to solve and finance its deficit position, in order to get that money, it had to do one thing, increase the interest rates. It is this increase in interest rates which has brought about the situation and the consequences which the small borrower and the small businessman find so difficult to meet.
On a point of order. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but he seems to be straying into another field entirely, that of fiscal policy, high interest rates, and so on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The fact that the committee has given unanimous consent to waive the rule of strict relevancy makes it hard to

say where the line should be drawn in the discussion of this subject of unemployment. I think the hon. member should be allowed to continue.
Surely financial and fiscal policy is strictly relevant to this discussion of unemployment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will only bear with me until I come to a conclusion he will see that there is a very close relevancy between financial and monetary policy and the situation in the field of unemployment as it exists today.
The consequence of this financial policy is that the service of the national debt has increased; it rose considerably. In fact, in this fiscal year, 1960-61, it will be $100 million more than it was a year ago. Because of that, and for the reasons I have given, the provinces, the municipalities and large corporations were obliged to borrow in the United States because they found the interest rates in the United States far more attractive than in Canada. By doing so, our foreign debt was increased.
The tight money policy has had a disastrous effect on small borrowers and on the small businessmen which this government was going to protect. In Quebec there were 50 per cent more bankruptcies in 1959 than in 1958, and because of that position, which was announced not by myself but by the clerk of the superior court of the district of Quebec, who made the statement himself and said it was due to the credit restrictions of the present government-
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No. At the end of my speech, but not now.
The government's monetary policy, by these restrictions, is supposed to fight inflation. The government's fiscal policy, by its deficits, has contributed directly to increasing the menace of inflation. There is a flagrant contradiction between the two policies of the government, and this has brought about a thoroughly inflationary situation and a tremendous increase in the cost of living-2 per cent per year since the present government took office. These are the policies which have brought about, directly and indirectly, the present unemployment situation in a large measure-tight money, high interest rates, an increase in the cost of living, credit restrictions. Are you surprised, therefore, Mr. Chairman, that the government is at its wits' end and does not know what to do; that it is asking those of us who sit on this side of the house for concrete proposals?

Either it stands up on its feet and meets the position-because it is the responsibility of the government, and not of those who sit on this side of the house -under our constitution the responsibility of dealing with a situation such as this, which is a serious one, is the minister's; it lies exclusively with him and his government and with his supporters on that side of the house-or it fails.
The minister has himself admitted his abysmal failure; his incapacity to submit anything concrete, and he has called on us to submit to the house concrete proposals. Now I ask the minister if he will not give serious study to these proposals and if, instead of making the kind of excited speech which he made the other evening, he will not during the course of this debate try to deal with our suggestions in a more constructive way.

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to speak on this item but in view of some of the observations made by hon. members who have participated in this debate, and particularly those observations which related to the province of New Brunswick, I feel compelled to make a few remarks. I appreciate the privilege of following the hon. member for Laurier and I have listened with a great deal of attention to his contribution. I should like to tell the hon. member now that for many years I have held for him a great deal of admiration and respect not only for his ability as a satesman but for his competence as a lawyer and public speaker. I hope that some of my remarks will not be considered by that hon. gentleman to apply to him directly.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Gloucester is not in his seat as I had some remarks that I felt applied to him and to the province which he represents. As one hon. member stated the other day, there has been a tendency among some of the maritime members to come to this parliament and indicate that the provinces in these Atlantic areas are poor cousins of the rest of Canada instead of those hon. gentlemen getting together and making our true position known.
I appreciate the invitation extended by the hon. member for Gloucester to get together in that connection but in view of the

remarks he has made in this committee from time to time regarding the situation in New Brunswick I do not put too much stock in his invitations.
The hon. member referred at various times and in various ways to the winter works program provided for in the item of $15 million which is presently under discussion. The unemployment situation is not a new one and of course is not to be taken lightly but I suggest to hon. members that it cannot be solved by our putting thousands upon thousands of words on the official record of this place and by creating screaming headlines in newspapers across the country. The problem can be solved only by each and every one of us-and we are supposed to be the leaders and representatives of the people- getting together to produce some constructive proposals.
The unemployment problem did not develop overnight. I can tell the hon. member for Gloucester that in the 40's I made many surveys in the maritimes for the Department of Public Works and conditions in Gloucester were just as bad if not worse than they are at the present time.
I was particularly interested when the hon. member for Kent spoke on the agriculture item. I can recall when potatoes in New Brunswick could not be sold for 70 cents a barrel but had to be dumped. That was not under a Conservative regime and so the government cannot be blamed for all the ills and troubles that are being experienced at the present time.
The province of New Brunswick is dependent primarily on primary industries, namely fishing, lumbering and, to a lesser extent, on agriculture. As a result of our primary industries we tend at times to have a certain amount of seasonal unemployment. We must try to establish in New Brunswick and throughout the entire Atlantic areas secondary industries that will provide some means of lessening the impact of seasonal conditions on employment.
The hon. member for Gloucester referred to the winter works program as inadequate. Is it inadequate from the standpoint of the program or from the standpoint of the unwillingness or inability of the county of Gloucester to take advantage of it. I suggest to the hon. gentleman that possibly a drive to collect $1 million in delinquent taxes in the county might enable it to have additional funds with which to undertake projects under this program. During the past year Gloucester county took advantage of the program to the extent only of $13,000, while in the same period the little county of Charlotte which I represent took advantage of it to the extent of $28,000.

The hon. member for Gloucester jumped from the province of Nova Scotia and read several articles from La Presse. He did not, however, read to this committee an extract from the January report of the unemployment insurance regional director in the city of Moncton. With the permission of the committee I should like to place a few extracts from this report on the record. The report refers first to my county of Charlotte. I am reading from extracts from the report as they appeared in the St. Croix Courier of February 18, 1960:
Fish processing and woods operations were at a high level in Charlotte county at the end of January, it was reported in Moncton last week by the regional director of the unemployment insurance commission.
R. P. Hartley, Q.C., in his regular monthly review of the employment situation in the province, said excellent fish catches in the Charlotte area had resulted in a "much improved situation" with five factories now employing a total of 700, compared with one plant in operation for the same period a year ago.
The report then refers to the snow conditions to which reference was made by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska and then goes on to point out that the position this year so far as New Brunswick is concerned is much better than it was a year ago.
The subsequent paragraphs of the report, I believe, bear out my contention that to supplement the primary industries in the maritime area we must have secondary industries of such a nature as will take up the slack in the seasonal unemployment. I am not suggesting for one moment that the present unemployment situation is caused solely by the seasonal aspect of it but I do suggest that in the Atlantic area particularly a large percentage of the unemployment at the present time is due to the nature of our industries.
In the county of Charlotte the unemployment situation is considerably less than it was a year ago. An editorial which appeared in the St. Croix Courier of February 25, 1960, states:
There are approximately 500 fewer people looking for work in Charlotte and part of York counties now than at the same time in 1959, statistics of the local national employment office disclosed Tuesday.
I might say that the registration district of the unemployment insurance commission for Charlotte county includes part of the constituency of York-Sunbury. I continue:
A bureau news release listed the number of unplaced applicants registered at the Water street office now at 2,245 compared with 2.722 for the same period last year. The current list is made up of 1,667 men and 578 women.
I point that out because the women listed as unemployed are women who are normally 79951-0-105

employed in the canning industry. Mr. Hartley summed up the situation in this way:
Reviewing the over-all employment picture, Mr. Hartley said conditions in the province, as reflected by the number of job applicants registering at national empolyment offices, were still somewhat better than a year ago.
The hon. member for Gloucester did not tell the committee of the increase in mining work in the constituency of Gloucester and of the possibility that a $17 million or $18 million smelter would be erected in that area. He referred to the Conservative promise of public works. I should like to point out to him that under this government he has received in his constituency more money for public works, public buildings and harbours and rivers than at any time when the previous administration was in office. I should like to give the figures to the committee. In 1958-59, up to March 31 of that fiscal year, not including any dredging, there was spent in the constituency of Gloucester, $603,442.04, and my information is that in that year there was spent for dredging an amount that would increase the total amount spent to over $1 million. In the previous year, 1957-58, when this government was in office, there was spent in that constituency $583,433.64. At no time previous to that was there anything like that amount spent. I say that this government has fulfilled any promises or any commitments that it made in respect of public works in the constituency of Gloucester.
From time to time, on the basis of unemployment figures, the hon. member has also inquired as to the coal situation in the province of New Brunswick. I refer to the mines at Minto. According to the latest report, the Minto mines are able to sell all the coal that can be mined in that area. I point these things out not to indicate for one minute that I am, or anybody else is, wholly satisfied with the situation as it now exists in the province of New Brunswick. The hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska indicated with some vehemence and heat the conditions in his constituency. I can sympathize with him; I know the conditions there almost as well as he does, since that is my native county.
I suggested-and I again suggest-that in addition to this winter works program we must endeavour by means of adequate electric power to bring secondary industries to the province of New Brunswick so that we shall have industries to absorb people who are laid off seasonally. Hon. members know that except under exceptional circumstances you cannot fish during the winter season although this year as I have indicated, we are most

Supply-Labour
fortunate in that we are running five factories where last year we ran only one, and shortly we shall open another. Within a month it is expected that the largest fresh filleting plant at Beaver Harbour will open, but we must provide some industries, some small payrolls, which will take up the seasonal unemployment.
I should like to suggest to the minister that in so far as this winter works program is necessary, and in so far as I can see it will be necessary for some time to come, consideration should be given to its extension so that it will become a little easier for certain municipalities temporarily short of funds to enter into the program. I would suggest that in the case of large capital expenditures involving considerable capital, such as the installation of sewers and water mains, the government consider increasing its contribution to the material items of these projects. I would also suggest that possibly-and I pass this on to the minister-the government should consider making it available to schools and school boards so that they could take advantage of this assistance to provide additional classroom space and do certain necessary repairs and alterations. I realize there are certain difficulties in connection with this proposal but I believe that through the municipalities and the provincial government this matter could be sufficiently straightened out.
I would also suggest-and in this I agree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate-that we should give further assistance in the training of young people in vocational guidance so that they will be able to adapt themselves to changing economic circumstances and be able to provide themselves with an assured means of income. It has been definitely established that the bulk of the people unemployed consists of those who did not go sufficiently far in school to qualify for higher education or for a better job. These are the people whom we should try to help so that we shall make worth-while citizens out of them.
Unemployment affects not only the man who is out of a job but also his home. If he is a young man of 20 or 21 he probably has to live with his parents and that increases the burden on them. He is not able to set up his own home or build his own house, and so on. Therefore, we have not only a falling off in the purchase of consumer goods but also their production, and we have an impact on the whole strata of society. In other words, unemployment lessens the standard of the Canadian way of life which we all want to have and should have.

I should also like to make another suggestion to the minister. If at all possible there should be a further extension of the winter works program so that incorporated towns might be encouraged to build fire halls and other public buildings. I realize that in certain municipalities the number of towns is limited and it might be difficult to have a municipality or an incorporated village assume this responsibility, but I suggest this is one thing that should be considered by the Department of Labour.
I would also suggest, and this is only a practical detail, that provision should be made for the announcement of the winter works program earlier in the current season; and that the privilege be given to those who wish to take advantage of it of starting their works at a time in the fall when they can be done economically without waiting for severe frost and winter conditions to set in. I have some knowledge of what it is like trying to do summer work in the winter time because it was my privilege during the last war to be the engineer in charge of the Pennfield airport and I can assure hon. members that trying to put down sewer and water lines at 30 degrees below zero is no fun. I suggest that if possible the program be announced earlier in the year and that the municipalities and towns have their applications approved so that they can start work even before the period now covered by the winter works program.
I did not come to this house as the representative of Charlotte to make political speeches. I came with the intention of making some contribution if I could on behalf of the people of my constituency and the province in which I was born and in which I have lived for most of my life. I think that should be the goal of each and every one of us. The unemployment problem is not one that can be solved by a few people. We as Canadians must solve it and we can only solve it by working together. Over the years the unemployment problem has continued to increase. Shortly after the end of the second world war there was a definite increase in unemployment and it has continued to increase except in certain areas.
I appeal to each and every member of the house not only to support the winter works program and the money now being voted for it but to endeavour by precept and example to encourage in the minds of our people a realization of the necessity of assisting themselves by trying to establish the secondary industries to which I referred.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to have the occasion to speak immediately after the hon. member who has just resumed

his seat because he began his remarks by stating that there is no point in placing hundreds of thousands of words on Hansard but instead we should try to establish methods to do away with the constantly and possibly increasing problem of unemployment. How can this be done unless the opposition, with all the strength at its command advises the Minister of Labour and the government of ways and means by which this will be accomplished?
We all realize that in this debate tempers have been quite high, but in the face of the remarks of the Minister of Labour last evening, when he said that the opposition had at no time brought forward any constructive suggestions as to methods by which the problem under discussion could be met, I state that the opposition is forced to go on and bring to the minister's attention such means as we may think of. I appreciate the effort of the hon. member who just sat down to try, even as a member of the government party, to tell the Minister of Labour the ways and means by which he can solve the unemployment situation which definitely creates much suffering in our country.
The Minister of Labour last night made a statement to the effect that the opposition was taking too much time on this matter which we consider important, and in that regard may I point out the fact that out of eight speakers who spoke on unemployment yesterday only three were from the Liberal opposition, four spoke on behalf of the government and one on behalf of the C.C.F. group. In the face of this fact surely it cannot be said that the Liberal opposition should not be allowed sufficient time to explain to the minister, who is crying out for information, any thoughts that we may have on the matter.
I appreciated very much the speech of the hon. member for Laurier this afternoon when he went to the extent of enumerating once again to the Minister of Labour the 25 suggestions made by the opposition during the course of the debate. If there has been any time lost surely it is obvious that the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot and the hon. member for St. Mary played their part yesterday. We heard it said that in no way was the government responsible for the present situation. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot stated that it was true that two manufactures had closed down in his constituency-
Replaced by four.

-but that was not the responsibility of the government in any way. In no way could this be tied up to the financial 79951-0-105 J
Supply-Labour
policies of the government but rather the reason for the closing of these two industries was that the ladies now wanted stockings without seams. Surely this was time lost. He was followed by the hon. member for St. Mary who made a purely political speech. He referred at length to the forthcoming election in the province of Quebec and at one stage he became so involved in his political speech that he referred to you, sir, as ladies and gentlemen.
Surely we must bring a more serious approach to this problem, and in an effort to do so I as a backbencher am prepared to try to give two suggestions to the Minister of Labour as to how I feel the problem should be met by the government. I consider the problem of unemployment definitely one of the most important facing us at this time. Why? Because unemployment is a criterion by which one can analyse the efficiency of the policies of the present administration and measure the prosperity of the country. I realize that on our statute books there is provision for unemployment insurance. That measure has a definite purpose but the country cannot exist and grow if we rely only on the unemployment insurance fund. I realize that people are happy to get the benefits of this legislation which was introduced by a Liberal administration but they do not wish to remain at home and only receive unemployment insurance payments.
We have spent two days in the house discussing the death penalty. I realize the importance of that matter but we have had the death penalty since confederation and surely if we can afford to spend two days on that subject at a time when we are faced with unemployment we should be able to consider the question of unemployment properly. We all realize that the matter of changing the Criminal Code with respect to the death penalty can wait another three weeks or a couple of months for decision. What is the problem with respect to unemployment?
I say that it is twofold. First, there is the value of the earnings to the person who receives a salary. We have heard something about that and that is the first reason that we wish to solve the unemployment problem, in order to be certain that the father of a family can receive a salary which will enable him to take care of his dependents.
However, there is another factor to consider in connection with unemployment and that is the factor of production. If we have a country in which people for long months or possibly for years contribute absolutely nothing toward production, then we know that our situation is deteriorating. I am not interested too much in statistics, and I do

Supply-Labour
not wish to be involved in this argument as to who is responsible for the problem. The only value which statistics have in this matter is to show that unemployment is a Canadian problem, that unemployment is increasing, and that should be sufficient in so far as the use of statistics is concerned. They have served their purpose when we have made up our minds about that.
What are the causes of unemployment? I say that if the government makes a full study of unemployment they will realize that the responsibility for it rests with it. A moment ago the hon. member for Laurier attempted to discuss the fiscal policies of the government as they were tied in with the question of unemployment. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka raised a point of order to the effect that such a discussion would be outside the realm of this debate. I am sorry the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka is not here at this time because at this time I should like to show him that, according to his own Prime Minister, unemployment is tied in with the financial problems of this country. I should like to quote from a Canadian Press report which appeared in the Ottawa Journal and is dated February 15, 1958, The report contains remarks made by the Prime Minister at Prince Albert on February 14, 1958, and here is what that report says:
The Prime Minister said here Friday night his Conservative government inherited the unemployment problem from a Liberal administration which "failed to act when it was warned."
"We are defeating the problem," he said. Figures for the last few weeks showed a slower rate of increase in unemployment.
"Where did unemployment come from? In the first place because we tied our economy too closely to the United States, losing our markets everywhere else. Second, because small businessmen were strangled by the tight money policy of the former government."
It is clear, Mr. Chairman, that the complete reply is given to the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka by his own Prime Minister and that unemployment in this country is necessarily tied up with other fiscal problems.
I was very interested in the reference made by the hon. member for Laurier to the problems and policies in connection with uranium. My riding is not so far from Elliot Lake, and I know the problems we have in connection with uranium today are the cause of the situation at Elliot Lake. I say that the Minister of Labour, and possibly the entire government, as was suggested by the Liberal opposition, should sit down and study this problem.
After having discussed the problem itself and its causes, may I ask what we are doing

about it? There is this measure that is before us now. I recall that it was rather shortly after my election when I first heard of this winter works program. How did that come about? Once again we saw the government in action as we have seen it in other phases of the winter works program. I recall that the announcement of the program was made at a political meeting out west. Nobody knew what it was, and what happened after that? I have copies of the telegrams that went forward because we find the telegram method was used concerning the winter works program just as it was used in connection with Avro. The premiers of the provinces were sent telegrams about this winter works program. I would think that, this would indicate how little thought was given to the program before a decision was made concerning the solution of the unemployment problem in Canada.
I have always considered the Minister of Labour to be a very kind man with a very good disposition. The only exception to this was a few minutes in this debate. I should think that the approach of the Prime Minister to this unemployment problem at the time of the election campaign, the promises made by the Prime Minister, coupled with the good nature of the Minister of Labour, would give this country what is required for a study of this most acute problem. There is no doubt about that.
I should like to cite how important it was for the Prime Minister of this country to solve this unemployment problem during his approach to the electorate. We have heard repeatedly how the unemployment problem was inherited from the Liberal party. I am not interested in such a discussion. I think when a government has been in power for three years, when it has promised it would solve this problem absolutely and we now see it rising again, there is no merit in discussing the question of inheriting a problem.
When I hear some hon. members from the government side stating that there is absolutely no unemployment at this time, that the situation is much improved, then I think if you hired someone to build up statistics on this matter you would find there are a great many Conservative members in this house who will tell you there is no problem. There are people who have said during the course of this debate that the unemployment problem was inherited from the Liberals. Surely there must be one, and only one answer to this. I think we are entitled to ask the minister, the Prime Minister and the government to tell us which it is in 1960.

If we know the problem and its causes, how are we going to measure the situation and how are we going to build up the determination to solve it? I should like to quote the words of the Prime Minister with regard to how he was prepared to measure the mination to solve it? I should like to quote in the Toronto Star concerning a political speech made by the Prime Minister at Brantford on February 17, 1958:
He charged the Liberals were trying to "All Canadians with fear" by saying there were 800,000 Canadians out of work. The actual number, he contended, was only half that.
Surely, at that time, if the Prime Minister had occasion to state that someone was referring to 800,000 unemployed, it is possible that his vision was too short to see that under his own regime in February, 1960 that would be the number of unemployed people.
How are we going to measure the situation? If that was an argument during a political campaign, it should be today an absolute argument to the Prime Minister to get down to work and to try to solve this problem but not necessarily by the scheme we have before us.
This afternoon when the hon. member for Laurier made the speech which he had occasion to make and indicated to the Minister of Labour the 25 suggestions at least which were indicated by the Liberal opposition, the hon. member for Parry Sound objected to certain of them. I must state that the riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka is immediately to the south of my riding. For the purpose of my future contentions I should like to give a few figures-but they will be very few- concerning the problem of unemployment in my riding and also, in order to assist the committee, I will give the figures for the riding of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka which is immediately to the south of mine in order that the committee will have a clear-cut picture of the unemployment situation in these two ridings.
In the riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka as far as the labour force is concerned, it is a much smaller agency that the government has there. The agency which covers Parry Sound has a labour force of 5,100 persons only. It covers only 2,230 square miles. The agency of government which covers in full my riding, although my riding is only a part of the agency established in Sudbury, has a labour force of 44,000. It covers 21,000 square miles and is roughly ten times larger than the unemployment agency in the riding of Parry Sound.
I will give you a few figures. I have obtained the figures for both agencies of the government for the month of January or
Supply-Labour
rather at January 31, 1960, which was the last date for which figures were available and also January 31, 1957, which was the last January of a Liberal administration. The figures are these. The unemployed at the agency of Sudbury on January 31, 1957 was 2,363; in Parry Sound it was 444. On January 31 of this year, 1960-and these are the last figures available from these agencies-the figure is 5,070 in Sudbury and in Parry Sound 861. In both ridings unemployment in January of those two years has risen over 100 per cent.
Surely this would indicate that the problem is not getting less but is definitely getting worse. That is why I wish to indicate to the Minister of Labour and to this committee that that is what the Canadian people are worried about and know about. The figures are definitely increases. I am not wishing to base my entire remarks on statistics, but surely these figures will indicate that the problem is definitely rising, that the problem in both these ridings-one which is represented by a Conservative member and one by a Liberal member-is getting worse and that unemployment has risen 100 per cent in each case. The figures for unemployment in January this year are double what they were in 1957.
I have looked at the record and the committee is fortunate that the Minister of Labour at one stage a few days ago was forced into tabling the details of the employment the winter works program would give to the citizens or the unemployed. I have made a check in order to see what it meant in my riding for those 5,070 and I have made a check of what it would mean in the Parry Sound area, taking the large municipalities as a measure-and I have done this in Parry Sound. In the city of Parry Sound this program provides absolutely no jobs whatsoever. I have checked Gravenhurst. This program creates no jobs in Gravenhurst in the riding of my friend, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. This program provides absolutely no jobs in Hemsworth. The program will provide six jobs in Huntsville. It will provide five jobs in Bracebridge; or in other words a total of 11 jobs, according to the perusal I have made in those centres.
I have checked my own riding of Nickel Belt and I find that in Capreol, Gorson, Levack, Creighton, Chelmsford, Blezard Valley, Hamner and Rayside, no jobs would be provided. Those are big centres in my area. In Coniston there is one program which will give 11 jobs to the unemployed there. This number happens to be the same as that which I mentioned in the riding of my friend the hon. member for Parry Sound. Surely this is no solution to the problem of unemployment if the matter is important.

Supply-Labour
It is important if we consider what has been achieved in other countries such as England and elsewhere. They are not faced with the same unemployment problem and this has not been explained by the government. They are not faced with the problem of unemployment to the same degree as we are, and that is something that should be explained by the government at this time.
If the problem is definitely a difficult one, if the problem is as we see it, unemployment has risen in these two ridings and those are the only two I had the time to study. The figure in those two has been doubled. In speaking about the percentage of unemployment according to the labour force in the riding of Parry Sound-since apparently some of the members would like to have more information-it is 17 per cent; 17 per cent of the labour force is unemployed. In my riding the figure is 13 per cent. Surely that fact is significant.
Is it not time that we tried to give to the municipalities a program which will fit in with their own. I realized when I checked the list that if you take from last year to this year, many municipalities when they first heard of this telegram and this possibility of 50 per cent went into some of these schemes. But if you check this year, most of the municipalities which had programs last year, have none this year. This should be an indication to this government that there is something lacking and missing in this program. If it is so worthwhile for municipalities, why would they not be back this year, those who had some last year? Why should we see most of them off the list this year? That is roughly the position in my riding.
What I say is this. The municipalities have programs but they have programs of their own, programs which have a significance in their area or locality. They have constructions they must make. They would probably be prepared to make them in the winter months if they obtained a few dollars from the federal government. But what type of work has been going on under this winter works program? I have heard comments and read articles indicating that members of councils were most displeased at being forced into works programs in which they have no intention of getting involved, just in order to try to get the 50 per cent bonus from Ottawa. But they are not repeating that procedure this year. If we are going to pay something, why should we not pay it. This is the proposition put to the Minister of Labour.
Why should we not pay something toward worthy projects put forward by the municipalities-projects initiated by the citizens

themselves concerning the construction of various buildings? Let us pay the labour costs of such constructions. The citizens of these municipalities would then have something which they want. Instead, we have brush cutters; we have people cutting branches along creeks and ditches. Mr. Chairman, how can you cut branches along a ditch in the wintertime when there is five feet of snow? These things are of no value at all, but this is the type of program the municipalities are forced to undertake because we will only pay half of the labour cost. Let the municipalities pay for the materials, but let us give them the opportunity to improve their cities and townships as they see fit. If this were done I am sure the programs undertaken would be more numerous than they are now. I am sure the government realizes that although there are 5,000 or more unemployed in my area, only one contract has been applied for under this scheme. It is evident that this scheme by no means meets the need.
I say, in closing, as I see that my time is expired, that what is needed now is a total study in this country of the whole employment field with the assistance of all those persons we have in our employment offices, all those people in charge of labour unions and all those people in industry who can help to solve this problem of rising unemployment. I recommend to the Minister of Labour that this should be a complete study, a sound study which will give this government the advice and opinion of every citizen who has something to contribute toward the solution of the present serious situation.
