If I can rely on what the Prime Minister said about unemployment-and I take it that the statement of the Prime Minister would be a sufficient answer for the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour-the right hon. gentleman said that deficit or no deficit, unemployment would be met at all costs.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, in launching this new discussion on unemployment, the Liberals have again failed to rouse public opinion against the government. They kept harping on the same old note they had struck during the sessions of 1958 and 1959.

I have always been astonished to hear their loud protests whenever we seek to establish the responsibility for today's employment conditions. They hasten to exclaim that the problem does not lie in that direction and that, instead of trying to discover who is responsible for the present situation, we should try to settle the problem. I share this view with the reservation however, that the Liberals should be the very ones not to express such an opinion because they are to a high degree responsible for the situation which this government has to face.
Those conditions are due to a lack of foresight in Liberal policy and developed during the war years, when the Liberals, in the smug enjoyment of an artificial prosperity, did not choose to act at the proper time to forestall the present situation that was foreseeable as far back as 1950. And, as the Liberal party is trying to make a scapegoat of the Conservatives, we might perhaps wonder, under the circumstances, what those people did when they had to face a serious unemployment situation.
If we go back to the year 1935, Mr. Chairman, we find that, at that time, we were up against an extremely difficult economic situation. In 1935, the Liberals who had abused the people, as they indeed have on various occasions since, got themselves elected on the formal and specific promise-
(Text):
No one will suffer. (Translation):

-to settle the unemployment situation and to check the recession.
Now, what did they do from 1935 to 1939, to remedy the depression? What positive steps did they take to face the disastrous economic conditions at that time? It seems to me that conditions were not much improved on the eve of the 1939 war, because, as we may recall, the province of Quebec had been forced, in 1936, to resort to special legislation for the relief of citizens affected by the depression. Then came the war, and the Liberals were well served by the turn of events. The state of war served them well, because, during that time, large numbers of citizens who had been unable to find work before 1939 found jobs and were able to earn their living.
That wartime situation went on until 1950, when the threat of unemployment began to worry the Conservative party, which then
Supply-Labour
demanded that the Liberal government take positive steps for the return of Canada's economy to a peacetime basis.
Once again the events in Korea, the threats of war which were still being felt at the time, saved the Liberals.
Each man for himself.

They had a rude awakening in 1957, when the difficult economic situation forced them to think and realize that the criticisms then made by the Conservative party were justified; and it is precisely because people realized that the Liberals had not managed to live up to the situation in the 1950's that they accordingly asked another group of citizens, another team of public men, to take over the administration of Canada's business.
Mr. Chairman, we cannot in the space of two or three years, correct a situation resulting from twenty-two years of lack of foresight and haphazard policy, which could not give Canada's economy an impetus, a leadership based on the economic facts of Canada's position in the North American context.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, it is with great interest and astonishment that I listened to the numerous suggestions-twenty-five, I believe

made by the former member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier). The hon. member suddenly discovered measures which might correct the present situation. He went on to list a series of projects, suggestions which, all of them, it seems to me, are designed to correct some situations, some Canadian economic facts.
Well, if those suggestions are applicable to fundamental problems within the Canadian economy, I wonder why the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) could not make them at the proper time to his own government, so that today we would not be rushed into correcting-
The country was well administered at that time.

-things that could have been normally corrected, when the country was in an era of greater prosperity.
The whole attention, the whole debate is centred on a particular aspect of unemployment: the winter works program introduced by the Conservative government.
The opposition expects this winter works program to be a universal panacea, providing for all present requirements.

Supply-Labour
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that is considering the problem from a wrong angle. The winter works program, supported by the Conservative government, is simply one of the remedies which must serve to correct the present situation.
In order to correct those conditions, we must, at the same time, count on the general economic recovery which is felt throughout Canada today.
I would like, Mr. Chairman, to draw the attention of the house for a few moments on the issues which more particularly affect my riding of Roberval.
My colleague the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) referred to it at length last evening when he asked me to take part in this debate and to offer suggestions about the particular problems of my constituency.
There has been an attempt to magnify the unemployment situation in my constituency. The situation is not at all tragic, and I do not hesitate to say so. To understand it, we must study some facts.
First, what does the economy of the Roberval riding consist of? The people of my constituency are primarily farmers, and no one would deny that the agricultural situation in the province of Quebec is, at this time, excellent. There are of course a few things that need to be set right, there are some weaknesses, but we can say that, in general, the farmers are satisfied and that the Roberval constituency, like all others, shares in this prosperity of the agricultural class. Then, we have in the constituency, a number of woodsmen, people who earn their living in the forest, either as lumberjacks or as employees of various industries related to the lumbering industry. In that industry too, the situation is good, not to say excellent, because employment has been normal and regular with about the same number of people working last fall as in previous years, at the time of this so-called Liberal prosperity.
On the other hand, there are in my consti-uency, lumber and woodworking industries. They too are very prosperous, since none of them has closed down; on the contrary, employment has increased in that industry.
Who are those affected by unemployment in my constituency? I must first say that they are the unskilled workers, people with no standard technical trade and who, therefore, find it difficult to get work.

Mr. Chairman, I have in the past suggested measures to promote technical and industrial training for the young people in my constituency, so that they might readily find employment in industries which now require specialized technical skills.
The unemployment problem, as it exists in my district, is primarily a seasonal one, and, it is mostly woodsmen who are affected by it. However I must say that conditions in this particular field have greatly improved and are likely to improve further, in view of the fact that lumbering industries in the Chicoutimi-Lake St. John district, and particularly in Roberval county, are carrying out a program that will provide employment for the workers on a year-round basis. They are considering a formula that would enable workers to work throughout the year, whereas under the present formula, workers usually work six or seven months and then are unemployed for varying periods, depending on the season.
Last evening, Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the hon. member for Lapointe who, I do not hesitate to say, is one of my best friends. He belongs to a category of public men whom I respect and who deserve to be respected. My friend, the hon. member for Lapointe, mentioned yesterday-or rather, he quoted last night-a pastoral letter of His Eminence Cardinal Leger on unemployment. He pointed out the responsibility which devolves upon those in authority of taking an interest in the solution of the unemployment problem. However, he forgot to stress one fact. He forgot to show how, at the provincial level, the government of our province of Quebec has shouldered this responsibility in our district, and more particularly in my riding, by supplying a good many jobs to the residents of that area in the past two years.
Let me merely mention, as far as my constituency is concerned, some of the works that the government of the province of Quebec has undertaken to improve the employment situation. The Quebec government is building a big bridge at Mistassini; it is building a road section to the Mauricie, commonly known as the La Tuque road; it is also building a road section between Chambord and St. Andre, and it is building the Normandin road. All this, Mr. Chairman, must be added to the numerous schools, colleges and convents that were built in the last two years.

Last evening, the hon. member for Lapointe could have mentioned projects already undertaken by the Quebec government in his constituency, and in Chicoutimi riding, particularly work on the Ste. Anne-Tadoussac road, on a new road section between Jon-quiere and Larouche, and on various projects and road-building work in this area of the province of Quebec.
I simply point out, by the way, the construction activities in the field of public buildings, under the leadership of the Quebec government. I believe that, on that count, the hon. member for Lapointe had no reason to deplore any failure on the part of authorities to assume their responsibilities and to do all that is possible to meet the unemployment situation.
Mr. Chairman, one of the particular problems of my constituency is the lack of industries; besides, it is still one of the causes of unemployment in my area. I would simply ask here, in all honesty, the following question to my friends of the Liberal party: What industries are there in the constituency of Roberval, that have been set up in the last 22 years? What are the new industries set up by the Liberal party in the constituency of Roberval? None at all, Mr. Chairman, because on that count, industries in our province are privately owned, and belong to private citizens. It is private enterprise or private initiative which is responsible for the new industries now existing in Roberval county.
It seems to me that the hon. member for Lapointe and other members of his party might have made suggestions to their government, in 1957, with a view to improving industrial conditions in the constituency of Roberval. Mines have been developed in that area, thanks to the government of the province of Quebec; unfortunately, development was delayed by the construction of the Chibou-gamau-St. Felicien railway, a delay for which the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) was largely responsible, as I indicated last year.
If you take a good look at the employment situation in the constituency of Roberval, I think you will find it is not much more serious than a few years ago.
In that connection, may I refer to a speech made by my predecessor in the house, Mr. Georges Villeneuve, on January 27, 1955. Here is what he said on the unemployment problem, and I quote from page 614 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I find that in my constituency unemployment does not cause as much concern now as it did last year. However, we do have
Supply-Labour
seasonal unemployment and it is a problem which requires our attention as well as all our ingenuity if we want to solve it.
What was stated in 1955, at the time of the Liberal prosperity, I am allowed, I hope, to state again today, since we have inherited this difficult situation from the Liberal party.
Before I conclude, Mr. Chairman, I should like once again to remind my colleague from Lapointe of certain statements he made in a speech on television during the 1958 election campaign. He stated at the time that the Liberal party should feel largely responsible for unemployment and he said, among other things-and I report his words in substance, I think-that the Liberals had fallen asleep when they were in office, that they should change course and that it was precisely because they had neglected the people and their problems that the people had withdrawn the trust they had put in that party.
Moreover, Mr. Chairman, not later than a few weeks ago, the same hon. member, speaking on T.V. in the Chicoutimi-Lake St. John area, pointed out that the unemployment situation in our district today was perhaps due to the fact that some negative criticism had been voiced with regard to the industries of our part of the country, and had thus adversely affected our industrial development.
In drawing attention to those speeches and remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Lapointe, it is not merely to pick a quarrel, but because I want him to join forces with the government in order to improve the employment situation and urge our Chicoutimi-Lake St. John area to seek a greater share of the general prosperity of this country, and enjoy other industrial developments than those it had under Liberal rule.

I rise on a question of privilege. I just heard the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay) give some sort of paraphrase of a speech I am supposed to have made in 1958 on a television broadcast. I shall get the text of my speech because it was certainly recorded, and I shall claim the privilege of repeating here exactly what I did say, because the hon. member did not at all quote the very words I then used.

I reported substantially what my hon. friend said.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened very carefully through the simultaneous translation system to the remarks made by the previous speaker, the hon. member for

Supply-Labour
Roberval. After listening most carefully to what he had to say-and I am certain the translation was correct-I can only say this: when, oh, when, are we going to arrive at the time in this session when the government as a government and government members supporting the government are going to stop blaming the government failures on what occurred under the Liberal administration?
You, yourself, Mr. Chairman, must have noted that we have been in session now for almost two months. We have been sitting here in this house for almost two months and we have not done very much so far. What do we find, Mr. Chairman? We find government members on the front benches or members like the hon. member for Roberval who just sat down explaining the failure of the government to deal with problems on the basis of what the Liberals did prior to 1957. The government has been in office since 1957 and surely we have reached that time when the Conservatives can stop damning the Liberals and the Liberals can stop referring to everything said by the Conservatives when they were on this side of the house. Surely in this session we have reached the stage when we can get down to business, forget the past and deal with the present.
It was my privilege to speak in this debate last Friday. I had no intention of getting up again but felt definitely impelled to do so because of the statements made by the Minister of Labour last night when I think, for a little while, he forgot himself. Because he was under attack by certain members of the official opposition the Minister of Labour felt obliged to rise and to go so far as to make charges. He did not differentiate in any way whatsoever in what he had to say. There are two parties in the opposition, one the official opposition and one this party, the effective opposition.
Last night the Minister of Labour referred to the opposition benches and made statements which the C.C.F. members cannot let pass unchallenged. I certainly am not going to let them go by without having something to say about them. I am directing what I have to say now to the Minister of Labour who said last night that nobody in the opposition during the six or seven days discussion of unemployment had made any contribution or suggestion with respect to the problem of unemployment. I have no right nor do I take the right to speak on behalf of the official opposition but I do say, and I do not do this very often, that there were suggestions made by the official opposition. I also say that all members of the C.C.F. party have spoken in this debate and we

have all made suggestions as to the unemployment situation with respect to what action should be taken both from a short range and a long range point of view.
I challenge the Minister of Labour to go over Hansard, check the speeches of members of the official opposition and those of the C.C.F. members and then say that no suggestions were made. But the fact is that the Minister of Labour refuses to accept any suggestion to deal with unemployment made by the official opposition or the C.C.F. unless it is something with which he agrees. If he does not take the view that he accepts it, then in his opinion no suggestion has been made. In my estimation that attitude is deplorable and despicable. Since when has it been the case that only the Conservatives have suggestions to make?
We are a democratic parliament and I am most amazed that the Minister of Labour cannot recognize the existence of any suggestions unless it happens to be something that he can personally accept. I held the Minister of Labour in high regard until his speech last night but last night he went right down into the gutter. He who thinks and prates so much about democracy nevertheless takes the position that no suggestion has been made unless it is something that he wants to accept. If that is the minister's understanding of democracy and parliament, then the sooner he is out of parliament the better for democracy in Canada.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

Would it be fair to say that most of the suggestions emanating from the C.C.F. have been virtual socialism and would it be fair, if you admit that, to say that the Minister of Labour cannot be expected to accept suggestions which are pure socialism? I do not say all the suggestions but a substantial number of those coming from the C.C.F. are virtual socialism.

That is a very nice question and I am glad the hon. member asked it. We in the C.C.F. are socialists and proud of it. Our objective is the establishment some day of democratic socialism in this country. But we are also eight representatives of the people sitting here as elected members of parliament dealing with day to day problems, and on every matter that comes before the house we put forward proposals that we think are in the interests of the welfare of the people of Canada.
When the Minister of Labour spoke last night he said that no proposals had been put

forward from the opposition benches to deal with the problem of unemployment. We put some forward and so did the official opposition which is not a socialist party. But because they are proposals which are not acceptable to the government the Minister of Labour says that no proposals were put forward. I say that is a despicable and rotten attitude to be taken by a cabinet minister who says that he believes in democracy and therefore believes in the right of members of opposition parties to make representations. What really got me and, indeed, was the main reason for my getting to my feet this afternoon, was this statement made by the Minister of Labour last night. I am glad he is looking at me and not talking to his colleague. Last night, he made a statement which I think was one of the rottenest I have ever heard made at any time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is three times you have said that now.

That is right, and I am going to repeat it half a dozen times before I sit down. I should like to hear the hon. member speak constructively from his feet instead of interrupting while sitting on his backside. As a matter of fact, I can now understand the report in Maclean's magazine to the effect that some of the Conservative backbenchers are getting heavy in the rear end.
Shame, shame.

Attribute the shame to the man who wrote it and not to me. I want to say that was one of the most despicable, rottenest statements I have ever heard from a man for whom I previously had the highest regard, that is until last night. I am referring to the statement made by the Minister of Labour to the effect that the opposition-he did not differentiate between the official opposition and the C.C.F.-were trying to make political capital out of unemployment and laughing- those were the words-at the unemployment situation.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

Yes, later. I am referring to the problems facing Canadian industrial companies in world competition; what they have to do to get greater efficiency and the planning necessary to take care of the workers.
In one moment I will answer questions, but I have only so much time and I shall be glad to answer questions when I sit down. When are you going to face up to the developments taking place in the capitalist world? When are you going to face up to what is happening in so far as exports are
Supply-Labour
concerned, when we are an exporting country. You never heeded the warnings so far as Fernie was concerned or so far as Elliot Lake was concerned, and now you have 10 months' notice that another company is going to close up, to consolidate for greater efficiency. The question is, what about the workers? How about planning between the government, industry and labour, so that when this sort of thing which is now happening in St. Catharines and which, by the way, is going to take place on an increasing scale, does occur plans will be ready to take care of it? When will these things be done on a basis which will take care of the workers who are being displaced and put them in new industry?
I am very sorry that this is happening in St. Catharines, but this just adds to what I tried to say last Friday. I did my best, I will tell the hon. member for York-Scarborough, to emphasize the essentiality of long range planning so that in the interests of efficiency the workers are cared for. I want to say-
Would the hon. member permit this question?
As soon as I am through you can ask all the questions you like, but not until I am finished.
Are you afraid of the question?

I said I will stay here and I will stay here as long as the Chair will allow. I hope you will ask questions fast and furious, and so long as the Chairman will give me time for you to question me and for me to answer, then I shall continue. However, I am limited now in the length of time I can speak. However, I am not limited with regard to how long I can answer questions. Therefore you are not going to catch me there.
I came into politics some 27 years ago. I know what it means to be unemployed. I want to tell the minister through you, Mr. Chairman-I am waiting, sir, until the Minister of Labour can listen-that he did something last night that I, as one of eight socialists out of 265 members, would never have done. I believe that no member of parliament, be he Conservative, Liberal or C.C.F., takes unemployment as a laughing matter. There is no one out of the 265 men and women who takes unemployment as a laughing matter. We are all concerned with the situation.
We in this party tried to ask the government to deal with the problem on the short range and long range basis. In particular, I want to draw your attention to what I said

Supply-Labour
last Friday. Last Friday when I spoke for the first time on this matter of unemployment I said this in the first two minutes, and I quote from page 1491 of Hansard for February 26, 1960.
We can read.

Perhaps you can read, but I am damned if you understand. I said this:
I have no Intention whatsoever, Mr. Chairman, of saying anything on charges and counter-charges as between the government and the official opposition on the responsibility for the problem. I have no intention, Mr. Chairman, of saying anything whatsoever on recriminations between the government and the official opposition on this matter, nor of saying one word about the private feud between two Conservative members in this House of Commons. I want to deal with this question of unemployment.
That is what I said, and I followed that out, as did every other member of this party. If the Minister of Labour will recall what I said on Friday, he will remember I referred to short range and long range planning. In particular I mentioned the long range and pointed out that problems are developing. I asked the government if they would face up to them. We have heard a great deal about Elliot Lake, about Fernie and about the coal mines on Vancouver island. However, this problem is brought even closer to home. There is an additional factor to which I tried to refer during questions on orders of the day.
It is no longer just a case of Fernie or of Elliot Lake or of the maritimes or of Vancouver island. We see capitalism faced with competition and having to close plants. John Inglis is closing its St. Catharines plant. An article in the Toronto Star states that the John Inglis Company Limited announced yesterday it will start immediately on the construction of a $2 million plant in Scarborough to handle the production now carried out at its St. Catharines plant. But it is going to close the plant at St. Catharines and 500 are going to be out of work by the end of the year. This has happened since last Friday when I spoke. We were asking that the emergency situation with regard to unemployment be taken care of, and we ask also, when are you going to face up to the developments taking place in your own capitalist system?
It is a short question.
It may be a long answer. May I continue?
You may.

I intend to do so whether the hon. member likes it or not. Through you, Mr. Chairman, may I tell the Minister of Labour that there is no member in this

house, irrespective of party, who treats unemployment as a laughing matter. It is a serious problem. Many suggestions have been made as to the handling of the unemployment situation and it does not become the Minister of Labour to say that the opposition puts forward no suggestions just because he does not like to accept them. The ideas and the propositions are there.
May I say that the evidence is now becoming increasingly clear of the seriousness of the situation of competition and the need for greater efficiency and production. That is going to hurt labour; but you cannot hurt labour too long. The time is now imminent. I am using St. Catharines as an example- and Elliot Lake-in the past and going beyond that. Will the Minister of Labour and the government not accept the constructive proposition to face reality, to plan for our greater efficiency, and for our operation on a more competitive basis in order to take care of the workers of this country? Whether the Conservatives like it or not, the workers are the ones who produce all wealth. For the minister to say that the members laugh is, I say, Conservative hypocrisy. I could use a stronger word but I do not want to be ruled out of order.
We are faced with a serious problem. I refer to the three parties in this chamber. There are 208 Conservatives, 48 Liberals and 8 C.C.F. I want to say this to the government. If you will get away from making charges as to who is responsible; if you will forget the past and will look at the present and the future; and if you will bring in something definite to take care of our unemployment and to take care of Canada, you will have the unanimous support of all members in this chamber. Have you patriotism to the people of Canada? Have you an understanding of the problem? Have you the guts to forget politics, to bring in unemployment measures and to discuss them on the basis of what will make a greater Canada and greater security for every person in our country?
The challenge is there. The decision is up to you. But because you are the government, with 208 members, only you have the power to move. Will you move? That is the question we are asking. Will you move? Will you quit your talking and indulging in wishful thinking and bring down definite policies? If you do so, this party will back you right down the line. If you do not do so, we are going to criticize constructively. I am going to tell the Minister of Labour that we are not the ones who are laughing. You are the ones who are cynical; and while you are being cynical and charging the opposition with laughing,

people are going hungry in this country. That is not what they were promised in 1958 and in 1957.

There are only a couple of minutes left until six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, but during that short time I should like to say that I feel this far-ranging debate on unemployment, on this most serious domestic problem before us, is one in which all hon. members, if they so wish, should have an opportunity to take part, and I intend to take part in it. May I say that I respect as much as does any hon. member the sincerity of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. I know how deeply he feels with regard to this problem and other social and economic problems. However, my respect for his sincerity does not persuade me to agree with all the solutions to the problem which he puts forward or indeed with the way in which he puts forward his solutions.
Last night, in an intervention which I think was most unfortunate, the Minister of Labour challenged the motives of some of us, or all of us in the opposition, taking part in this debate. I regretted as much as did my hon. friend-in fact I deplored it-some of the words and the attitude of the minister at that time. But I may say that I did not consider that to be the normal attitude of the minister in this chamber and that I do not consider him in any respect to be a rotten or despicable person. Normally I think his attitude is not based on considerations of that kind. Over the years in this chamber I think he has won a reputation for sincerity and integrity. That is why we deplored all the more his intervention last night. I think that over the years the minister's attitude and approaches to this problem have not been rotten or despicable and I would not go as far as did my hon. friend a few moments ago in describing what happened last night. These things do occur. I think the minister lost his temper. His patience gave way.
Under provocation.

We have been charged with prolonging this discussion-although I certainly do not accept that charge and I have no apology to make for our party-and deliberately obstructing the passing of this item in the estimates.
What are you doing now?

Someone says "What are you doing now?" I am stating my position on the
Business of the House
most important domestic problem now before the Canadian people. If that is obstructing, I plead guilty to doing it.

MAJOR GENERAL M. H. S. PENHALE
speechtext:
1.	Does Major General M. H. S. Penhale, director of the civil defence college at Arnprior, report directly to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, in the matter of civil defence or does he report to the Prime Minister and/or the ministers of national defence or justice?
2.	Has Major General Penhale made a report to the government along similar lines to the material contained in his recent article which appeared in the Royal Canadian Air Force Staff College Journal?
3.	Is the government taking any action to arouse public interest in civil defence measures?
4.	If so, what specific measures are being taken to enlist the co-operation of provincial and municipal governments?
Answer by: Righl Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker
(Prime Minister):
1.	The Minister of National Health and Welfare.
2.	No.
3.	Yes.
4.	The specific measures taken for this purpose include:
(a)	The government has proposed to, and worked out with, the provincial governments an allocation of civil defence functions and responsibilities to be assumed by the federal authorities on the one hand and the provincial and the municipal authorities on the other.
(b)	Two federal-provincial conferences of ministers were held during 1959 to discuss and resolve questions of mutual concern regarding civil defence.
(c)	The dominion government has revised the basis of providing financial assistance to provincial and municipal civil defence projects and increased the proportion of the cost borne on federal appropriations from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. For the next fiscal year, 1960-61, the government has proposed to parliament an appropriation for financial assistance to provinces and municipalities in this field in an amount twice that which had been allocated in previous years.
(d)	Frequent consultations have been held between civil and military representatives of the dominion government on the one hand and ministers and officials of provincial governments on the other on the implementation of policies in the field of civil defence.
(e)	The Canadian army has allotted duties to many of its officers and units to assist the civil authorities in the preparations for civil defence responsibilities in wartime, and the army has undertaken special training and equipment of its units for these purposes.
(f)	Federal officers have been provided in each of the provinces to work with provincial authorities in developing plans and other preparations for emergency measures to be taken in wartime in those areas, including civil defence measures. Plans are now being developed with respect to the preparation of combined communication and related facilities to permit the effective functioning of governments at all levels in wartime emergencies.

subtopic: JACQUES CARTIER BRIDGE TOKENS
JACQUES CARTIER BRIDGE TOKENS
speechtext:
1.	Does the authority administering the Jacques Cartier bridge now use a toll system, based on tokens and machines?
2.	If so, what steps were taken to ensure that counterfeit tokens, slugs or other devices could not be used in the machines?
3.	Is supervision at the machines able to catch any attempts to use counterfeit tokens or slugs?
4.	If not, has later examination of the "take" indicated there is use, substantial or otherwise, of counterfeit tokens or slugs?
5.	If so, has action been taken in any way to handle this problem?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of
Transport):
The national harbours board advises as follows:
1.	Yes.
2.	(a) Counterfeit tokens, slugs or other devices will not actuate the toll collecting machine and register paid fare unless they are manufactured within the very strict tolerances for diameter and thickness of Canadian coins.
(b)	It is believed that the value of the tokens as a toll (8 cents) is too low to warrant the manufacture of counterfeit tokens to the exact tolerances required. It is estimated that the manufacture on a small scale of counterfeit tokens or slugs would cost approximately 6 cents each.
(c)	A newly developed device will shortly oe installed in the toll collecting machines in automatic lanes which will immediately detect the use of slugs regardless of accuracy of reproduction.
3.	(a) At attended lanes the toll officer in attendance can immediately detect the use of counterfeit tokens or slugs whether or not they are built to exact tolerances.
(b) At automatic lanes with present equipment, the bridge sergeant would detect the use of counterfeit tokens or slugs if they are not built to exact tolerances, since they would immediately register a violation which would sound a bell, indicating that a car had gone through the lane without payment of proper fare.
4.	The average number of slugs found in the reject box of the collection machines is approximately four per day, out of a total of approximately 45,000 tokens or coins registered daily. This, however, does not indicate that a patron depositing a slug in the machine has gained access to the bridge without paying the proper fare. It only indicates that an attempt was made to go through the lane by using a slug.
5.	(a) Patrons attempting to use slugs for payment of fare have been apprehended and in two cases legal action has been taken which resulted in fines of $50 in one case and $25 in the other.
(b) As indicated above in answer 2 (c), a newly developed device will shortly be installed in the toll collecting machines. This device will immediately detect the use of slugs.

subtopic: VETERANS DISABILITY PENSIONS
VETERANS DISABILITY PENSIONS
speechtext:
1.	Are any tax exemptions made for veterans in receipt of disability pensions?
2.	If not, has the government given any study to the American practice of exempting soldiers bonuses and veterans pensions for tax purposes?
Answer by: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister
of National Revenue):
1.	Yes. Section 10, subsection 1(d) of the Income Tax Act provides exclusion from income of any compensation paid under section 13 of the Pension Act for injury or disease, or any aggravation thereof, resulting in the disability or death of any member of the naval, military or air forces of Canada in respect of service therein during world wars I and II, or in respect of peacetime service therein.
In addition, section 10, subsection 1(e) of the Income Tax Act provides a similar exclusion from income of any compensation on account of disability or death resulting from war service received by a Canadian resident

from countries which were allies of His Majesty during world wars I and II and which granted substantially similar relief for the year to members of its naval, military or air forces as that provided for persons in receipt of a pension under the provisions of section 13 of the Pension Act. The countries that qualify for purposes of this particular subparagraph are as follows:
World war I: Belgium, Brazil, China, commonwealth countries, Costa Rica, Cuba, Czechoslovakia, Ecuador, France, Greece, Guatemala, Haiti, Hedjaz, Honduras, Italy, Japan, Liberia, Montenegro, Nicaragua, Panama, Poland Portugal, Rumania, Russia, San Marino, Serbia, Siam, United States of America, Uruguay, Yugoslavia.
World war II: Argentina, Belgium, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, China, Columbia, commonwealth countries, Costa Rica, Cuba, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Dominican Republic, Egypt, Ethiopia, France, Greece, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Iran, Iraq, Italy, Lebanon, Liberia, Luxembourg, The Netherlands, Nicaragua, Norway, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Poland, Salvador, San Marino, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Siam (Thailand), Turkey, United States of America, U.S.S.R., Uruguay, Venezuela, Yugoslavia.
The provisions of these two subparagraphs refer only to war service pensions received on account of disability or death and, as such, do not extend in any way either to payments on account of superannuation or to naval, army or air force long service pensions.
2.	Answered by (1) above.
